name: Aaron Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, twenty-seven, and I lead a two-person crew wiring homes and fixing shop electrics. My two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence got me into the difficult jobs early. I like leaving every cable labelled so the next person can understand the work; I dislike having a customer tell me a video says the job takes ten minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your situation away from the tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone in a small flat I own without a mortgage, and I've got eight months of expenses saved. The wage is high for this job, and there are plenty of other electrical firms around. I use AI occasionally for a first draft of an estimate explanation, after a colleague has checked the tool, but I still do my own testing and calculations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sensible firms can keep the tools that help and stop paying for the ones that don't. A good name still comes from turning up and leaving safe work behind. I wouldn't mind if customers stopped asking whether an app could replace the whole visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and income feel secure in that picture. Owning the flat and having eight months saved means I can handle a quiet spell, and there are other contractors nearby. I'd rather earn well at a trade I know than take a gamble just because someone else is excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same installation and repair work now and through the first year. I'd use the estimate-writing tool now and then, checking every sentence against my own figures. I'd leave my budget and savings plan as they are rather than invent a response to something that barely changes the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, almost grateful for the boring version. A steady week leaves room for Sunday lunch with my parents and a game of football afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sentence would you remove from an estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything saying the price cannot change before I've opened the old board. I can be clear about the starting price without making a promise that ignores what's hidden in the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel pressure to buy new technology because you can afford it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, when another contractor shows off a new subscription. I'd ask what job it does better than the tools I own. Having spare money isn't a reason to stop checking the bill.

say: I'd say **sensible firms** can keep useful tools and stop paying for tools that do not help.
I think **a good name** still comes from turning up and leaving safe work behind.
think: My **work and income** feel secure with higher pay and eight months of expenses saved.
My **mortgage-free flat** and nearby contractors give me room to handle a quiet spell without gambling on a new field.
do: Keep the **installation and repair work** now and throughout the first year.
Use the **estimate-writing tool** occasionally, checking every sentence against my own figures.
feel: **Calm**, enjoying a steady week with time for family lunch and football.
S0.quote: Having spare money isn't a reason to stop checking the bill.
fieldNote: His **financial security** combines higher pay, a mortgage-free home and existing savings, making continuity a plausible choice in the mild picture.
He uses **proven AI occasionally**, while refusing to buy another subscription simply because a competitor already has one.

steps.text: Keep wiring homes and repairing shop electrics on the usual rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the quicker firms win customers, provided the work is checked properly. I'd want every quote to say what has actually been tested, not hide behind a clever paragraph. Apprenticeships still matter because somebody has to learn the difference between a draft and a safe installation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own pay looks safe for the next few years because most of my job is physical work in awkward buildings. I am uneasy about bigger firms using cheap quotes to take the easy jobs and leave us the awkward ones. My flat is paid for, but I still need a business that pays wages, not just compliments about craftsmanship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd agree to a six-week paid trial of the quoting tool, but only after our estimator checks it against completed jobs. In the first year I'd keep a notebook of the actual hours on ten awkward repairs and compare them with the software's allowances. I'd stay on the same crew while the owner decides whether the numbers justify keeping the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though not frightened for my next pay packet. I want to know whether faster means fewer wasted hours or simply less money allowed for the difficult bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which awkward repair goes in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An old shop where the cable route disappears behind a fitted counter. Finding the route can take longer than replacing the damaged cable, and a tidy quote shouldn't make that time unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the estimator to check it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estimator sees far more finished prices than I do. I don't need the honour of finding every obvious error myself, and I'd rather use something a colleague has already tested.

say: I'd support **competition on price** as long as firms keep checking work properly.
I'd say **apprenticeships** still matter because someone must distinguish a draft from a safe installation.
think: My **own pay** looks safe while most work remains physical and buildings remain awkward.
I worry that **cheap quotes** could leave our firm difficult jobs with too little paid time allowed.
do: Join a **six-week paid trial** only after the estimator checks the tool against finished work.
Record actual hours for **ten awkward repairs** during the first year to compare with software allowances.
Stay with the **same crew** while the owner checks whether the system earns its cost.
feel: **Uneasy** about pricing difficult work, while the next pay packet still feels secure.
S1.quote: My flat is paid for, but I still need a business that pays wages, not just compliments about craftsmanship.
fieldNote: His **market outlook** accepts faster competition while insisting that real repair time and safety remain visible in the price.
A **colleague-tested trial** fits steady adoption; recording difficult visits gives him evidence rather than assuming all automation saves paid time.

steps.text: Trial the quoting tool for six paid weeks after estimator checks
Keep repair work and record actual hours on ten awkward visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2028 is close, but we should ask what a small firm can actually sell before declaring the trade finished. Planning goes first; robots doing the physical work arrive around 2031. I'd back employers who offer real paid apprenticeships instead of asking people to buy hope from a course website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could fall when larger firms can plan cheaply and later use robots for more of the fitting. Eight months saved and no mortgage mean I can choose carefully, not that I can stop earning at thirty-two. I don't know whether the smaller firms nearby would have vacancies after the same shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare advertised building-equipment service jobs now, asking two employers what training and guaranteed hours they actually offer. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply only where an advertised post includes paid practical training and a wage that covers my bills. I'd keep the current job until I have a written offer; meanwhile I'd add two hundred a month to savings if my income stays unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a plan I can put on paper. I'd rather be cautious with a contract now than proud about never changing and angry at an empty diary later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you turn an offer down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wage that depends on finding my own customers before I finish learning. I'd want the base pay, hours and travel costs written down, not just a top figure from the best month anyone has had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add savings when the flat is already paid for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because food, building charges and replacing a broken van still cost money. Saving another two hundred while I can is easier than assuming family will fill the gap later.

say: I'd ask what **small firms** can actually sell before declaring the trade finished.
I'd favour **paid practical apprenticeships** rather than a course website selling hope.
think: My **income could fall** as larger firms automate planning and later more physical fitting work.
My **savings and flat** buy choice, but nearby firms may face the same shock and stop hiring.
do: Compare **advertised service posts** now and ask two employers about training and guaranteed hours.
Apply after 2028 only for **paid practical training** with affordable wages, keeping the current job until a written offer.
Save **two hundred monthly** while current income and household bills allow.
feel: **Anxious but organised**, willing to compare contracts without rushing into a vacancy.
S2.quote: Saving another two hundred while I can is easier than assuming family will fill the gap later.
fieldNote: His **job search** depends on an actual post with paid practical learning, written hours and a wage that covers bills.
Owning **a flat** lowers one expense but does not remove living costs or justify assuming local employers remain immune to the shock.

steps.text: Apply after 2028 only for posted service jobs with paid training and affordable wages
Save two hundred monthly while income and bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for firms to show a proper ladder from apprentice to paid equipment work. I'd rather see three real posts with training than a room full of promises. Families can support someone learning, but they shouldn't be asked to finance a contractor's entire change of business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still lose well-paid repair hours, but I have more time to check another route before the thinking work changes in 2031. The robots follow around 2034, when I'll be thirty-five. I'd like to arrive there with some paid experience of different equipment, rather than only a course receipt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd set up a monthly transfer of two hundred to the emergency account while my bills allow. I'd ask for one supervised paid day a month on building-control servicing next year, keeping my current total wage and hours. In the first year after 2031 I'd increase those days only if the firm has real bookings and keeps those pay terms; otherwise I'd compare posted roles before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with more patience than in the two-year picture. Trying one paid day feels like a step I can judge rather than a bet on a whole new life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm has no servicing bookings next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't pretend there was a training job. I'd keep doing repairs and look at actual advertised roles, asking the same questions about wage and supervised learning before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to learn on that one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to identify a failed controller safely and replace it under supervision, following the maker's instructions. I wouldn't call myself trained because I'd watched someone connect a laptop once.

say: I'd ask firms for **real paid posts** with training rather than a room full of promises.
I think **family support** should not have to finance a contractor's whole business change.
think: My **repair hours could fall**, but five years gives me longer to check a different paid route.
I'd like **paid equipment experience** before robots arrive around 2034, rather than only a course receipt.
do: Save **two hundred monthly** while bills allow, using an automatic transfer.
Seek **one paid servicing day** monthly next year only with current total wages and hours kept.
Increase service days after 2031 only with **real bookings** and the same pay terms, otherwise compare posted roles.
feel: **Anxious but patient**, able to judge a small paid trial before making a larger change.
S3.quote: Trying one paid day feels like a step I can judge rather than a bet on a whole new life.
fieldNote: His **supervised learning** requires real service bookings and maintained total pay and hours, rather than an unfunded career promise.
The **monthly transfer** is new saving while income permits, distinct from simply retaining the reserve he already holds.

steps.text: Save two hundred monthly when bills allow
Seek monthly supervised servicing only with real bookings and maintained wages and hours
Compare posted service roles if internal paid work is unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can afford to be practical rather than dramatic. I'd keep telling young people to look for a good employer who pays while teaching, and to read the contract. A familiar trade can change without every bit of knowledge becoming useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and income look secure over the next few years in this slower picture. Thinking AI changes planning in 2036, with physical robots around 2039, when I'll be forty. I still need to prepare for a long working life. I don't feel I have to buy a new career this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing repairs now and ask next month about the same supervised servicing day, only with real bookings and unchanged total pay and hours. In the first year after 2036 I'd join a paid trial of the new planning tool after another crew tests it, checking the result against real work. I'd review job and training offers once a year, sooner if my paid hours start falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the worry has a place rather than filling the whole room. I can keep Sunday lunch and football while I learn what is actually changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a planning trial successful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plan would fit the real job without leaving safe checks or travel time out of the price. I'd want the crew to compare several completed visits, not just admire a quick drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy equipment yourself with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I later had customers, the full price and a repair agreement to compare. None of those figures exists for me today, so I'd keep my money rather than describe a purchase as a plan.

say: I'd recommend a **good employer** who pays during learning and puts the terms in a contract.
I think **existing trade knowledge** can still matter when familiar work changes.
think: My **near-term work** and income look secure, giving me room to prepare without buying an answer immediately.
At **forty in 2039**, I'll still need income after robots reach the physical work.
do: Seek **supervised servicing** now only with real bookings, unchanged total pay and hours.
Join a **paid planning trial** after 2036 only after another crew tests it against real jobs.
Review **job and training offers** annually, sooner if paid hours fall.
feel: **Uneasy but settled**, able to keep family lunch and football alongside preparation.
S4.quote: I don't feel I have to buy a new career this month.
fieldNote: His **steady adoption** waits for another crew's evidence and a paid trial, rather than turning a decade's warning into immediate technology spending.
He separates **possible future ownership** from a concrete action, because customers, machine prices and a repair agreement are not yet known.

steps.text: Seek supervised servicing only with real bookings and unchanged total pay and hours
Join a paid planning trial after another crew checks real jobs
Review offers annually, sooner if paid hours begin falling

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because a careful move between jobs takes time even when you have money put aside. Real paid training posts with written hours and wages would help. I'd also want clear course descriptions, so a person can see what equipment they'll touch before paying anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what an offer really pays after the travel and the unpaid hours. A new job can look like an escape on paper and still leave less money for the same life. I want to change when the work makes sense, not just when the headline frightens me.

headlineQuote: A new job can look like an escape on paper and still leave less money for the same life.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old crew lead** with a technical diploma and master licence, wiring homes and repairing shops.
He lives alone, earns **higher pay**, owns a mortgage-free flat and has eight months saved with many current employers nearby.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it, favouring contracts and small paid trials over a rapid change of field.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious about income**; longer warnings allow supervised experience with maintained pay and reviews of actual offers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time for a careful job move, even with money saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training posts** should state hours and wages in writing.
**Clear course descriptions** should show the actual equipment people will practise on before paying.
